objectives.text: Describe how new technologies led to changes in everyday life for Americans

readings.title: The Roaring 20s
readings.text:
The 1920s was a decade of exciting social changes and profound cultural conflicts. For many Americans, the growth of cities, the rise of a consumer culture, the upsurge of mass entertainment, and the so-called "revolution in morals and manners" represented freedom from the restrictions of the country's Victorian past. Gender roles, hairstyles, and dress all changed profoundly during the 1920s. But for many others, the United States seemed to be changing in undesirable ways. The result was a "cultural civil war," in which a society clashed bitterly over such issues as foreign immigration, evolution, the Ku Klux Klan, prohibition, women’s roles, and race.

The 1920s was the first decade to have a nickname: “Roaring 20s". It was a decade of prosperity and dissipation, and of jazz bands, bootleggers, raccoon coats, bathtub gin, flappers, flagpole sitters, bootleggers, and marathon dancers. It was, in the popular view, the Roaring 20s, when the younger generation rebelled against traditional taboos while their elders engaged in a lot of speculation.  It was known as the “Roaring 20s” for a variety of reasons - a reference to jazz, the economic growth, and luxurious lifestyle many indulged in.

readings.title: Is Technology to Be Celebrated?
readings.text:
Not everyone celebrated and welcomed technological change. Below are excerpts from the ongoing debate over whether technology improved lives or was a menace to intelligence and traditional ways of life.

CELEBRATE TECHNOLOGY!

• New inventions and new developments of inventions constantly press in. The people of the world are daily being drawn nearer together by increased rapidity of communication. No nation can be a laggard in such times as these. Every nation that hopes merely to keep its place, much more to forge ahead, must find its job and do it with all its power.

• All great inventions of this age have been time-saving inventions. They are great inventions because they save time. These uncanny contrivances machinate to accomplish in minutes what formerly took us hours, or even days. (Paradoxically, the more time-saving inventions you have about, the less time you have to spare; but that is beside the point.)

• Machinery has made possible the payment of a higher wage for shorter hours and less drudgery. Thanks to machinery, the common man enjoys today an amount of leisure undreamed of by his predecessors, lives, and brings up his family in a style which would have seemed to them almost princely. . . . The progress in mechanical invention has given something more than wealth and leisure. Cheap and rapid transport has enormously enlarged the human horizon. Travel, in the past, was a luxury which only the very rich could afford. . . . Today even the poor can take small journeys;

TECHNOLOGY IS RUINOUS

• We went through one of the big automobile factories today...The heat was terrific. The men seemed weary. Here manual labor is a drudgery and toil is slavery. The men cannot possibly find any satisfaction in their work. They simply work to make a living. Their sweat and their dull pain are part of the price paid for the fine cars we all run. And most of us run the cars without knowing what price is being paid for them.

• The existence of more machines than purchasing power to absorb their output has led to the foolish and expensive antics of high pressure salesmanship, and the growing danger of competitive imperialism. Machinery has created a new ruling class based on profits...Natural resources are being exploited at a rate as alarming as it is wasteful.

• The machine has deprived the housewife of her sometime skills, and so forced uncounted women into futility and neurotic unrest. It has also forced women into the wage-earning class, and thus launched the feminist movement. Feminism is hardly an unmixed blessing, but it will undoubtedly show a net gain in the ledger of history.

readings.title: The Radio
readings.text: Of all the new appliances to enter the nation's homes during the 1920s, none had a more revolutionary impact than the radio. Sales of radios soared from $60 million in 1922 to $426 million in 1929. The first commercial radio station began broadcasting in 1919, and during the 1920s, the nation's airwaves were filled with musical variety shows and comedies. Radio drew the nation together by bringing the same news, entertainment, and advertisements to more than 10 million households by 1929. The radio also created a new form of advertising.

readings.title: “Sudden Greatness”
readings.source: Kenneth Chafee McIntosh, The Atlantic Monthly, Sept. 1921
readings.text:
The airplane was not invented in the 1920s, but aviation seemed to be the future of travel, especially after Charles Lindbergh completed his solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927. Would air travel be a dream or a disaster?

The future [of aviation] is limitless, not predictable. It is daily demonstrating its ability to extend the scope of our economic fabric to lengths undreamed of, and in ways which were but yesterday fantastic dreams...it has forced us to take sober and urgent thought as to how this mighty and as yet irresponsible force may be subordinated (used) to the common good...The future of all the world is in the air—a future either glorious or terrible. Your generation and mine will decide which it shall be.

readings.title: Major Inventions of the 1920s
readings.text:
• The radio

• Washing machines

• Refrigerators

• Vacuum cleaners

• Assembly line

• The Model T Ford, Ford Model A Roadster, Rolls Royce Phantom, Cadillac Convertible

• The traffic signal

• Electric razors

• Movies, especially “talkies” after the 1927 hit The Jazz Singer (“talkies” are movies with sound)

• Penicillin (antibiotic)

readings.title: Age of Advertising
readings.text:
“Change is in the very air Americans breathe, and consumer changes are the very bricks out of which we are building our new kind of civilization,” announced marketing expert and home economist Christine Frederick in her influential 1929 monograph, Selling Mrs. Consumer. The book, which was based on one of the earliest surveys of American buying habits, advised manufacturers and advertisers how to capture the purchasing power of women, who, according to Frederick, accounted for 90% of household expenditures. New consumer products such as ready-to-wear clothing, processed foods, and home appliances flooded radio and poster ads. American businessmen attempted to keep up consumer demand by developing new merchandising and marketing strategies to make products not only constantly appealing, but also necessary. Advertising became an artform, and the radio and cinema provided new canvases.

On the following pages are collections of advertisements from the 1920s. Consider the strategies behind them: to whom were they trying to appeal and what messages did they attempt to convey to consumers?

files.caption: Henry Ford made the automobile affordable for the average American. By the 1920s, the growing “car culture” was changing the nation in deeper ways than even Ford might have imagined.
Automobiles encouraged the growth of related industries—especially the oil industry. The gas station—and gas fumes—became a permanent feature of the U.S. landscape.

By 1925, states had built hundreds of highways, and the federal government organized them into a numbered system. One of the first federal highways was Route 66, which ran from Illinois to California.
Americans used their new cars and expanded leisure time to travel. Motels and motor camps sprung up all over the nation.
Ads stressed what cars gave their owners—speed, status, and a new sense of freedom.

images.title: The Radio in the Living Room

files.caption: As more radios were sold, the radio became the centerpiece of millions of American living rooms. At first, headsets were required to listen to broadcasts.
Even for the majority of women who stayed at home to care for the house and children, life changed. New consumer products such as dishwashers and vacuum cleaners made housework easier.

By the 1920s, Americans were going to the movies so often that attendance at other forms of public entertainment, such as theater, suffered. Decades later, the rise of television would have the same effect on movie attendance.
No fad symbolizes the Roaring Twenties more than the Charleston. Here, two young people demonstrate the wild, loose-limbed dance that swept the nation.
Consumerism is a social, cultural, and economic phenomenon where personal happiness, social status, and economic health are tied to the continuous purchase and consumption of goods and services
Baseball remained America’s favorite sport, but mass media brought it to an entirely new audience.

Mass-market magazines with eye-catching covers were more popular than ever. This Life magazine cover (left) highlights the growing popularity of golf among both men and women. Amazing Stories (right) was the first “pulp” magazine devoted exclusively to science fiction.
